1.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **those complaining** speaks of people who make complaints, so the Israelites were actually doing this in **the ears of Yahweh**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [the people complained of evil in the ears of Yahweh]

Here, the word **evil** could go with: (1) **complaining** as its object. Alternate translation: [like those complaining about evil in the ears of Yahweh] (2) **in the ears of Yahweh**. Alternate translation: [like those complaining, and it was evil in the ears of Yahweh] (3) **complaining** as a descriptor. Alternate translation: [like those complaining bitterly in the ears of Yahweh]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [like those complaining that things were evil]

1.q: בְּ⁠אָזְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה וַ⁠יִּשְׁמַ֤ע יְהוָה֙ וַ⁠יִּ֣חַר אַפּ֔⁠וֹ
1.note: It might seem that the expression **in the ears of Yahweh** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [while Yahweh heard, and his nose burned]
The phrase **in the ears of Yahweh** means in Yahweh’s hearing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [while Yahweh could hear]

The phrase **his nose burned** is a common expression of this culture that means that Yahweh is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and his anger burned] or [and he was enraged]

1.q: וַ⁠תִּבְעַר־בָּ⁠ם֙ אֵ֣שׁ יְהוָ֔ה וַ⁠תֹּ֖אכַל בִּ⁠קְצֵ֥ה הַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶֽה
1.note: Here, the author could be implying that: (1) the fire burned the edges of the camp but did not kill anyone. Alternate translation: [and the fire of Yahweh burned among then, and it ate tents and belongings at the edges of the camp] (2) the fire burned in the camp near its edges and did kill some people. Alternate translation: [and the fire of Yahweh burned among them, and it ate some people at the edges of the camp]

The author is using the possessive form to describe a **fire** that was sent by **Yahweh**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the fire that Yahweh sent]

The author is speaking of **fire** as if it were a living thing that could eat or devour things. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it ravaged]

2.note: The expression **the fire sank** is a common expression of this culture to mean “the fire went out” or “the fire died down.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the fire went out] or [and the fire died down]

3.q: וַ⁠יִּקְרָ֛א שֵֽׁם־הַ⁠מָּק֥וֹם הַ⁠ה֖וּא תַּבְעֵרָ֑ה כִּֽי־בָעֲרָ֥ה בָ֖⁠ם אֵ֥שׁ יְהוָֽה
3.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [and because the fire of Yahweh burned among them, he called the name of that place Taberah]
The pronoun **he** could refer: (1) generically to anyone who used this name. Alternate translation: [and people called] (2) to Moses. Alternate translation: [and Moses called]

The word **Taberah** is the name of a place. This name sounds like the Hebrew word for “burning.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain this in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [the place of burning]
See how you translated this phrase in [11:1](ta:11). Alternate translation: [for the fire that Yahweh sent]

4.note: The implication is that there were some people among the Israelites who were not Israelites themselves and who were causing trouble by encouraging the Israelites to complain. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And some non-Israelite troublemakers that were]
The pronoun **its** refers to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in the midst of the people]

Here, the author is speaking as if the non-Israelite people were actually in the **midst** of all the Israelites. He means that the non-Israelites were living among the Israelites. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [among the people]

The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [had a strong desire]
By **a desire**, the author means a desire to eat meat. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a desire to eat meat]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desire**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what they desired]

The author is using **returned, and they wept** as a common expression of his culture to mean “they wept again.” The text in [11:1–2](ta:11) implies that they had already wept once. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [wept again]
The pronoun **they** refers to the Israelites who were complaining. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Israelites said]

The Israelites are using the question form to express their strong desire for meat. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [If only someone would feed us flesh!]

5.note: By **we**, the Israelites mean to include both themselves and their listeners, so use the inclusive form of that word if your language marks that distinction.

5.q: אֵ֣ת הַ⁠קִּשֻּׁאִ֗ים וְ⁠אֵת֙ הָֽ⁠אֲבַטִּחִ֔ים וְ⁠אֶת־הֶ⁠חָצִ֥יר וְ⁠אֶת־הַ⁠בְּצָלִ֖ים וְ⁠אֶת־הַ⁠שּׁוּמִֽים
5.note: The **cucumbers** and **watermelons** are kinds of gourds, and **leeks**, **onions**, and **garlic** are kinds of vegetables used for seasoning. If your readers would not be familiar with what these foods are, you could use more general terms or explain them in a footnote. Alternate translation: [the fruits with rinds, and the savory vegetables]

6.note: Here the Israelites speak as if their lives were **dry**. They could mean that: (1) they have lost their strength because they do not have enough to eat. Alternate translation: [And now we have lost our strength] (2) they have lost their appetite for food because they do not like eating only manna. Alternate translation: [And now we have lost our appetite]

In this verse, the word **life** is singular in form, but it refers to all the lives of the Israelites as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “life.” Alternate translation: [our lives are dry]
By **our**, the Israelites mean to include both themselves and their listeners, so use the inclusive form of that word if your language marks that distinction.

If it would appear in your language that the Israelites were making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [the only thing in our eyes is the manna]

The implication is that the people meant there was nothing worth eating except manna. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [there is not any food]

The people are using the common expression of their culture **in our eyes** to mean “that we can see” or “that is available to us.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that we can observe]

7.note: Here, the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. The phrase **And the manna** introduces an explanation of the manna, how it appeared, and what the people did with it in 11:7–9. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [Now about this manna:]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the seed of coriander** is small and round, so is **the manna**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [it was small and round like the seed of coriander]

The author is using the possessive form to describe **seed** that is from the **coriander** plant. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [coriander seeds]

The plant named **coriander** produces leaves that people use for seasoning and call “cilantro.” It also produces small, round seeds that are 3–5 millimeters in diameter. If your readers would not be familiar with what **coriander** is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the small, round seed of a plant called coriander]

The point of this comparison is that just as **bdellium** is yellowish-brown in color, so is **the eye** (the appearance) of the manna. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and it was yellowish-brown, like bdellium]

Here, **eye** represents appearance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and its appearance was like the appearance of bdellium]

A **bdellium** is a kind of gum resin that comes from certain trees. If your readers would not be familiar with what bdellium is, you could use the name of a similar resin that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [a gum resin called bdellium]

8.q: שָׁטוּ֩ הָ⁠עָ֨ם וְ⁠לָֽקְט֜וּ וְ⁠טָחֲנ֣וּ בָ⁠רֵחַ֗יִם א֤וֹ דָכוּ֙ בַּ⁠מְּדֹכָ֔ה וּ⁠בִשְּׁלוּ֙ בַּ⁠פָּר֔וּר וְ⁠עָשׂ֥וּ אֹת֖⁠וֹ עֻג֑וֹת וְ⁠הָיָ֣ה טַעְמ֔⁠וֹ כְּ⁠טַ֖עַם לְשַׁ֥ד הַ⁠שָּֽׁמֶן׃ וּ⁠בְ⁠רֶ֧דֶת הַ⁠טַּ֛ל עַל־הַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶ֖ה לָ֑יְלָה יֵרֵ֥ד הַ⁠מָּ֖ן עָלָֽי⁠ו
8.note: If it is more natural in your language to indicate how the manna appeared before indicating what the people did with it, you could move the information from verse 9 before the information in verse 8. You would then present the combined verses as 11:8–9. See the UST for an example.

8.q: וְ⁠לָֽקְט֜וּ וְ⁠טָחֲנ֣וּ בָ⁠רֵחַ֗יִם א֤וֹ דָכוּ֙ בַּ⁠מְּדֹכָ֔ה וּ⁠בִשְּׁלוּ֙ בַּ⁠פָּר֔וּר
8.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they gathered the manna, and they ground it in the mill or crushed it in the mortar, and they boiled it in the pot]

A **mill** is a kind of stone tool used for grinding grain. A **mortar** is a stone bowl in which people would crush grain. If your readers would not be familiar with what a mill or a mortar is, you could use more general terms or explain them in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and they ground with stones that they used for grinding grain or crushed in bowls with special stones]

Here, **mill** and **mortar** represent grinding tools in general, not specific grinding tools. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and they ground in mills or crushed in mortars]

Here, **cakes** are a kind of bread baked in a flat, round shape. If your readers would not be familiar with what cakes are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [flat, round loaves]

The author is not referring to a specific **oil**. He means oil in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [oil]

9.note: The author is using **came down** as a common expression of his culture to mean “settled” or “formed.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And when the dew condensed in the camp]

The implication is that when the dew came down at night, the manna appeared along with it. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the manna was there along with it]

10.note: The previous verses include background information about the manna. Here, the author returns to the main storyline. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a form that makes this explicit. Alternate translation: [Now when the people said those things, Moses heard]

The author is not referring to a specific **man**. He means all the men in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [each of the men at the openings of their tents]

Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [a person at the opening of his or her tent]

The phrase **the nose of Yahweh burned** is a common expression of this culture that means that Yahweh is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh’s anger greatly burned] or [and Yahweh was very enraged]

The phrase **in the eyes of** is a common expression of this culture that means “in the judgment of” or “in the opinion of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and in the judgment of Moses]

Here, the author could mean that Moses considers **evil**: (1) what the people did. Alternate translation: [what the people did was evil] (2) that the people made Yahweh angry. Alternate translation: [it was evil that the people made Yahweh angry] (3) that Yahweh was angry. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s anger was evil]

11.note: The implication is that Moses went to the tent of meeting to speak with Yahweh. This is shown clearly when it says “And Moses went out” in 11:24. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And Moses went to the tent of meeting and said]

11.q: לָ⁠מָ֤ה הֲרֵעֹ֨תָ֙ לְ⁠עַבְדֶּ֔⁠ךָ וְ⁠לָ֛⁠מָּה לֹא־מָצָ֥תִי חֵ֖ן בְּ⁠עֵינֶ֑י⁠ךָ לָ⁠שׂ֗וּם אֶת־מַשָּׂ֛א כָּל־הָ⁠עָ֥ם הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה עָלָֽ⁠י
11.note: Moses is using the question form to express strong negative emotions and to complain about his situation. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [You are doing evil to your servant. I clearly have not found favor in your eyes, since you have put the burden of all this people on me.]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [do you harm your servant]

Moses is speaking of himself in the third person as **your servant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [to me, who serves you]

Moses is using the common expression of his culture **found favor in your eyes** to mean “gained your approval” or “pleased you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [do you not approve of me] or [do you not show me favor]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **favor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [am I not favored in your eyes]

Here, Moses is speaking of his responsibility to care for the Israelites as if it were a heavy **burden** that he had to carry. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to make me work very hard to care for all this people]

12.q: הֶ⁠אָנֹכִ֣י הָרִ֗יתִי אֵ֚ת כָּל־הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה אִם־אָנֹכִ֖י יְלִדְתִּ֑י⁠הוּ כִּֽי־תֹאמַ֨ר אֵלַ֜⁠י שָׂאֵ֣⁠הוּ בְ⁠חֵיקֶ֗⁠ךָ כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר יִשָּׂ֤א הָ⁠אֹמֵן֙ אֶת־הַ⁠יֹּנֵ֔ק עַ֚ל הָֽ⁠אֲדָמָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר נִשְׁבַּ֖עְתָּ לַ⁠אֲבֹתָֽי⁠ו
12.note: Moses is using the question form for emphasis and to express his frustration at being expected to care for the Israelites like a mother. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [I, I did not conceive all this people. I, I did not bear him, that you say to me, ‘Carry him in your bosom just as the one nursing carries the one sucking,’ upon the ground that you swore to his fathers.]

12.q: הֶ⁠אָנֹכִ֣י הָרִ֗יתִי אֵ֚ת כָּל־הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה אִם־אָנֹכִ֖י יְלִדְתִּ֑י⁠הוּ
12.note: Here, Moses is speaking as if he were actually **a mother** who had conceived and given birth to all the Israelites. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Am I like a mother who conceived all these people? Am I like the mother that bore them]

Moses is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verbs translated as **I conceive** and **I bear** already include this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it is definitely not he who did those things. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that emphasis. Alternate translation: [Was it I who conceived … was it I who bore him]

12.q: שָׂאֵ֣⁠הוּ בְ⁠חֵיקֶ֗⁠ךָ כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר יִשָּׂ֤א הָ⁠אֹמֵן֙ אֶת־הַ⁠יֹּנֵ֔ק עַ֚ל הָֽ⁠אֲדָמָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר נִשְׁבַּ֖עְתָּ לַ⁠אֲבֹתָֽי⁠ו
12.note: Here, the quotation could end after: (1) the word **sucking**. Moses speaks the rest of the sentence to Yahweh. See the ULT. (2) the word **father**. This implies either that Moses **swore** the promise or that Yahweh is speaking about himself in the second person. Alternate translation: [‘Carry him in your bosom just as the one nursing carries the one sucking upon the ground that you swore to his fathers?’]

12.q: כִּֽי־תֹאמַ֨ר אֵלַ֜⁠י שָׂאֵ֣⁠הוּ בְ⁠חֵיקֶ֗⁠ךָ כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר יִשָּׂ֤א הָ⁠אֹמֵן֙ אֶת־הַ⁠יֹּנֵ֔ק עַ֚ל הָֽ⁠אֲדָמָ֔ה
12.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [that you tell me to carry him in my bosom just as the one nursing carries the one sucking, upon the ground]

Here, Moses is speaking as if the Israelites were actually a **child** whom he had to **carry in his bosom** and nurse. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Take care of them as if you were carrying them in your bosom … to their fathers]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the one nursing carries the one sucking** is gentle and caring, so Moses should care for the Israelites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [with the tenderness of a nurse carrying the one sucking]

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply the words “to give to” from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [that you swore to give to his fathers]
Moses is using the term **fathers** to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to his predecessors]

Moses is using **over the ground** as a common expression of his culture to mean “to the land.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the place]

13.q: מֵ⁠אַ֤יִן לִ⁠י֙ בָּשָׂ֔ר לָ⁠תֵ֖ת לְ⁠כָל־הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה כִּֽי־יִבְכּ֤וּ עָלַ⁠י֙ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר תְּנָ⁠ה־לָּ֥⁠נוּ בָשָׂ֖ר וְ⁠נֹאכֵֽלָה
13.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [These people weep upon me, saying, ‘Give to us flesh and let us eat.’ But from where is meat for me to give to all this people?]

13.q: מֵ⁠אַ֤יִן לִ⁠י֙ בָּשָׂ֔ר לָ⁠תֵ֖ת לְ⁠כָל־הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה
13.note: Moses is using the question form to emphasize that it would be impossible for him to get enough meat to feed all the Israelite people. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is no place for me to acquire meat to give to all this people.]

The phrase **upon me** is a common expression of this culture that means “near me” or “to me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [near me] or [to me]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [demanding that I give them flesh so that they can eat it]
Here, the word **saying** introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated **saying** in [1:1](ta:01).

14.q: לֹֽא־אוּכַ֤ל אָנֹכִי֙ לְ⁠בַדִּ֔⁠י לָ⁠שֵׂ֖את אֶת־כָּל־הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה כִּ֥י כָבֵ֖ד מִמֶּֽ⁠נִּי
14.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since **heavy from me** gives the reason for the result that **I myself am not able by myself to carry all this people** describes. Alternate translation: [Carrying all this people by myself is heavy from me. So, I, I am not able to do it]

Moses is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I am … able** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he is definitely not able to do this. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that emphasis. Alternate translation: [I am certainly not able]

Here, Moses is speaking of the responsibility to lead and care for the Israelites as if it were a heavy object that he had to **carry**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to care for all this people]

Here, Moses is speaking of taking care of the Israelites as if it were a heavy **burden** that he must carry. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it is too hard for me to do]
Here, the word **heavy** could describe: (1) carrying the people. Alternate translation: [this burden is heavy] (2) the people. Alternate translation: [they are heavy]

15.q: וְ⁠אִם־כָּ֣כָה ׀ אַתְּ־עֹ֣שֶׂה לִּ֗⁠י הָרְגֵ֤⁠נִי נָא֙ הָרֹ֔ג אִם־מָצָ֥אתִי חֵ֖ן בְּ⁠עֵינֶ֑י⁠ךָ
15.note: Moses is describing a possible condition in which God will kill him only if two conditions are both true: God is going to continue treating him in this way, and Moses has found favor in God’s eyes. Express this possible condition in a way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Suppose that you are doing thus to me, and suppose that I have found favor in your eyes. In that case, killing, please kill me]

Moses is repeating forms of the verb **kill** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [please kill me immediately]

Moses is using the common expression of his culture **found favor in your eyes** to mean “you approve of me” or “you show me favor.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the negative form of this clause in 11:11. Alternate translation: [if you approve of me] or [if you show me favor]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **favor**, you could express the same idea in another way. See how you translated the negative form of this clause in 11:11. Alternate translation: [if I am favored in your eyes]

Here, Moses is speaking of his suffering as if it were his own **evil** that he needed to look at. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I do not want to experience my evil]

Moses is using the possessive form to describe **evil** that is happening to him. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [on the evil that is happening to me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [on the evil things that are happening to me]

16.note: A **officer** is a kind of leader with authority over others. If your readers would not be familiar with what an officer is, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and ones with authority over it]
In a context such as this, your language might say **bring** instead of “take.” Alternate translation: [and you shall bring them]

17.note: Here, God is speaking of his coming to Moses as if he would physically **come down** from heaven to earth. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will meet you]

17.q: וְ⁠אָצַלְתִּ֗י מִן־הָ⁠ר֛וּחַ אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָלֶ֖י⁠ךָ וְ⁠שַׂמְתִּ֣י עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֑ם
17.note: Here, Yahweh is speaking of the Spirit that empowered Moses as if it were a physical substance that could be **taken away** from one person and **put** on others. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will share with them some of the authority and power that I gave you through my Spirit]

On this issue, see the chapter introduction for more information. Here, the word **Spirit** could refer to: (1) God’s Spirit. Alternate translation: [from my Spirit] (2) Moses’ own spirit that Yahweh has specially equipped. Alternate translation: [from the spirit]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and I will put some of that Spirit on them]

Here, Yahweh is speaking of taking care of the people as if it were a heavy **burden** to carry. The image emphasizes how difficult and wearisome this responsibility is. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar metaphor in 11:11. Alternate translation: [and they will work hard to care for the people with you, and you, you will not have to care for them by yourself]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **the burden** that is made up of **the people**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the burden that the people create]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you will … carry** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Moses will definitely not need to do this. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that emphasis. Alternate translation: [and you will no longer carry]

18.q: וְ⁠אֶל־הָ⁠עָ֨ם תֹּאמַ֜ר הִתְקַדְּשׁ֣וּ לְ⁠מָחָר֮ וַ⁠אֲכַלְתֶּ֣ם בָּשָׂר֒ כִּ֡י בְּכִיתֶם֩ בְּ⁠אָזְנֵ֨י יְהוָ֜ה לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר מִ֤י יַאֲכִלֵ֨⁠נוּ֙ בָּשָׂ֔ר כִּי־ט֥וֹב לָ֖⁠נוּ בְּ⁠מִצְרָ֑יִם וְ⁠נָתַ֨ן יְהוָ֥ה לָ⁠כֶ֛ם בָּשָׂ֖ר וַ⁠אֲכַלְתֶּֽם
18.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And you shall say to the people that they must consecrate themselves for tomorrow, and they shall eat flesh, for they wept in my ears, asking who would feed them flesh and declaring that it was good for them in Egypt. Say to them that I shall give to them flesh, and they shall eat.]

18.q: הִתְקַדְּשׁ֣וּ לְ⁠מָחָר֮ וַ⁠אֲכַלְתֶּ֣ם בָּשָׂר֒ כִּ֡י בְּכִיתֶם֩ בְּ⁠אָזְנֵ֨י יְהוָ֜ה לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר מִ֤י יַאֲכִלֵ֨⁠נוּ֙ בָּשָׂ֔ר כִּי־ט֥וֹב לָ֖⁠נוּ בְּ⁠מִצְרָ֑יִם וְ⁠נָתַ֨ן יְהוָ֥ה לָ⁠כֶ֛ם בָּשָׂ֖ר וַ⁠אֲכַלְתֶּֽם
18.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **you shall eat flesh** with the information about **Yahweh shall give to you flesh**, since these are related events that are separated by the reason **For you wept in the ears of Yahweh**. Alternate translation: [Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, and Yahweh shall give to you flesh, and you shall eat it. For you wept in the ears of Yahweh, saying, “Who will feed us flesh? For it was good for us in Egypt.”]

18.q: הִתְקַדְּשׁ֣וּ לְ⁠מָחָר֮ וַ⁠אֲכַלְתֶּ֣ם בָּשָׂר֒ כִּ֡י בְּכִיתֶם֩ בְּ⁠אָזְנֵ֨י יְהוָ֜ה לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר מִ֤י יַאֲכִלֵ֨⁠נוּ֙ בָּשָׂ֔ר כִּי־ט֥וֹב לָ֖⁠נוּ בְּ⁠מִצְרָ֑יִם
18.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since **For you wept in the ears of Yahweh** gives the reason for the result that **consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, and you shall eat flesh** describes. Alternate translation: [You wept in the ears of Yahweh, saying, “Who will feed us flesh? For it was good for us in Egypt.” So, consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, and you shall eat flesh.]

Here, **in the ears of** represents that Yahweh heard what the people said. See how you translated this phrase in [11:1](ta:11). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [while Yahweh could hear]

The Israelites are using the question form to express their strong desire for meat to eat. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [If only someone would feed us flesh!]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is the reason why they asked the question. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [We ask that because it used to be]

It might seem that the expression **Yahweh shall give to you flesh, and you shall eat** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language since Yahweh has already said that they will eat flesh. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh shall give to you flesh]

19.q: לֹ֣א י֥וֹם אֶחָ֛ד תֹּאכְל֖וּ⁠ן וְ⁠לֹ֣א יוֹמָ֑יִם וְ⁠לֹ֣א ׀ חֲמִשָּׁ֣ה יָמִ֗ים וְ⁠לֹא֙ עֲשָׂרָ֣ה יָמִ֔ים וְ⁠לֹ֖א עֶשְׂרִ֥ים יֽוֹם
19.note: If you decided in the previous verse to translate this quotation in such a way that there would not be a quotation within a quotation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [Say to them that they shall eat not one day and not two days and not five days and not ten days and not 20 days]

19.q: לֹ֣א י֥וֹם אֶחָ֛ד תֹּאכְל֖וּ⁠ן וְ⁠לֹ֣א יוֹמָ֑יִם וְ⁠לֹ֣א ׀ חֲמִשָּׁ֣ה יָמִ֗ים וְ⁠לֹא֙ עֲשָׂרָ֣ה יָמִ֔ים וְ⁠לֹ֖א עֶשְׂרִ֥ים יֽוֹם
19.note: The implication is that Yahweh will give them meat for a much longer time than any of these shorter periods. Yahweh lists increasingly longer periods of time to emphasize that Yahweh will give them more meat than they expect. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [You shall eat not just for one day or two days or five days or ten days or 20 days]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [You shall eat flesh]

20.q: עַ֣ד ׀ חֹ֣דֶשׁ יָמִ֗ים עַ֤ד אֲשֶׁר־יֵצֵא֙ מֵֽ⁠אַפְּ⁠כֶ֔ם וְ⁠הָיָ֥ה לָ⁠כֶ֖ם לְ⁠זָרָ֑א יַ֗עַן כִּֽי־מְאַסְתֶּ֤ם אֶת־יְהוָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּ⁠קִרְבְּ⁠כֶ֔ם וַ⁠תִּבְכּ֤וּ לְ⁠פָנָי⁠ו֙ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר לָ֥⁠מָּה זֶּ֖ה יָצָ֥אנוּ מִ⁠מִּצְרָֽיִם
20.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [until a month of days, until when it goes out from their nose. Say to them that it shall be for nausea for them because they rejected me who is in their midst, and they wept to my face, asking why they went out from Egypt.]

The implication is that they would eat meat for 30 days. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [but for a month of days] or [but for 30 days]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **a month** that is made up of all its **days**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all the days in a month]

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if the meat were actually **going out from your nose**. This means that they will become very sick of the meat. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [until when you are too full] or [until when you gag on it]

Yahweh is not referring to a specific **nose**. He means their noses in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [from your noses]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **nausea**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And it shall make you nauseous]
Here, **to his face** represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before him]

The people are using the question form to complain about leaving Egypt and to express their regret that they left. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [We should never have gone out from Egypt!]
It might seem that the word **this** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [Why did we go out]
In a context such as this, your language might say “came” instead of **went**. Alternate translation: [we came out]

21.note: The implication is that this number represents only the adult men who could walk, since the census in Numbers 1 only counted adult men. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [are 600,000 men on foot, plus the women and children]

The number **600,000** is a round number, since 1:46 indicates that there were 603,550 men. Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [six hundred thousand]

The phrase **on foot** is a common expression of this culture that means “who walk.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who walk]

21.q: וְ⁠אַתָּ֣ה אָמַ֗רְתָּ בָּשָׂר֙ אֶתֵּ֣ן לָ⁠הֶ֔ם וְ⁠אָכְל֖וּ חֹ֥דֶשׁ יָמִֽים
21.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [but you, you said that you shall give flesh to them, and they shall eat a month of days]

Moses is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you said** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh was the one who said this. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that emphasis. Alternate translation: [but you definitely said]

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they shall eat flesh]

Moses is using the possessive form to describe a **month** that is made up of all its **days**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. See how you translated this phrase in 11:20. Alternate translation: [all the days in a month]

22.q: הֲ⁠צֹ֧אן וּ⁠בָקָ֛ר יִשָּׁחֵ֥ט לָ⁠הֶ֖ם וּ⁠מָצָ֣א לָ⁠הֶ֑ם אִ֣ם אֶֽת־כָּל־דְּגֵ֥י הַ⁠יָּ֛ם יֵאָסֵ֥ף לָ⁠הֶ֖ם וּ⁠מָצָ֥א לָ⁠הֶֽם
22.note: These two phrases **Shall flock and cattle be slaughtered for them, and it shall find for them** and **shall all the fish of the sea be gathered for them, and it shall find for them** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Shall flock and cattle be slaughtered for them or all the fish of the sea be gathered for them, and it shall find for them?]

22.q: הֲ⁠צֹ֧אן וּ⁠בָקָ֛ר יִשָּׁחֵ֥ט לָ⁠הֶ֖ם וּ⁠מָצָ֣א לָ⁠הֶ֑ם אִ֣ם אֶֽת־כָּל־דְּגֵ֥י הַ⁠יָּ֛ם יֵאָסֵ֥ף לָ⁠הֶ֖ם וּ⁠מָצָ֥א לָ⁠הֶֽם
22.note: Moses is using the question form for emphasis to point out the impossibility of what God had promised to do. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [Were flock and cattle to be slaughtered for them, it would not find for them. Or were all the fish of the sea to be gathered for them, it would not find for them.]

22.q: הֲ⁠צֹ֧אן וּ⁠בָקָ֛ר יִשָּׁחֵ֥ט & אֶֽת־כָּל־דְּגֵ֥י הַ⁠יָּ֛ם יֵאָסֵ֥ף
22.note: The expressions **be slaughtered** and **be gathered** are passive verbal forms. If your language would not use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Shall someone slaughter flock and cattle … shall someone gather all the fish of the sea]

The phrase **it shall find for them** is a common expression of this culture that means “it will be enough for them” or “it will satisfy them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it satisfy them … and it satisfy them]

23.note: Yahweh is using the question form **Is the hand of Yahweh short?** to strongly emphasize that he is fully able to do what he has promised. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The hand of Yahweh is not short!]

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if he had a **hand** that could be too short to reach what he wanted. He means that his power is not limited. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Is the power of Yahweh limited?]
Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as **Yahweh**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [my hand]

The word **you** is singular here because Yahweh is speaking directly to Moses. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction. Alternate translation: [Now Moses, you will see whether my word will happen to you or not]

Here, **see** represents experiencing or knowing something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Now you will experience]
Here, **word** represents what Yahweh said he would do. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what I said]

24.note: The implication is that Moses went out of the tent of meeting where he had been speaking with Yahweh. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And Moses went out of the tent of meeting]
In a context such as this, your language might say “came” instead of **went**. Alternate translation: [And Moses came out]
Here, **words of Yahweh** represents what Yahweh said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what Yahweh had spoken]

25.note: Here the author is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a person who could move up and down in space. This was a common way of describing God appearing to humans to interact with them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 11:17. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh met them]

The implication is that this was the same cloud that represented Yahweh’s presence, which descended on and remained above the sacred tent as described in 9:15–23. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the cloud that was over the Dwelling]

25.q: וַ⁠יָּ֗אצֶל מִן־הָ⁠ר֨וּחַ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָלָ֔י⁠ו וַ⁠יִּתֵּ֕ן עַל־שִׁבְעִ֥ים אִ֖ישׁ
25.note: Here, the author is speaking as if the **Spirit** that empowered Moses were a physical substance that could be removed from one person and distributed to others. This represents God sharing his power and authority. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar construction in 11:17. Alternate translation: [and he shared some of the authority and power that he gave Moses through his Spirit with 70 men]

On this issue, see the chapter introduction for more information, and see how you referred to **Spirit** in 11:17. Here, the word **Spirit** could refer to: (1) God’s Spirit. Alternate translation: [from God’s Spirit … God’s Spirit] (2) Moses’ own spirit that Yahweh has specially equipped. Alternate translation: [from the spirit … the spirit]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. See how you translated the similar clause in 11:17. Alternate translation: [and he gave some of that Spirit on 70 men]

Here, the author is speaking of the Spirit as if it were a physical being that could **rest** on people. This represents God giving these men authority and power to serve as leaders. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as they received the authority and power through God’s Spirit]

The phrase **they did not add** is a common expression of this culture that means “they did not do it again” or “it happened only that one time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but they did so only that time]

26.note: The expression **were left** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And two of the men remained]
If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **the one**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [the first]

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **the second**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [the other] or [number two]

26.q: וַ⁠תָּ֧נַח עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֣ם הָ⁠ר֗וּחַ וְ⁠הֵ֨מָּה֙ בַּ⁠כְּתֻבִ֔ים וְ⁠לֹ֥א יָצְא֖וּ הָ⁠אֹ֑הֱלָ⁠ה וַ⁠יִּֽתְנַבְּא֖וּ בַּֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶֽה
26.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **they were among the written ones** with the information about **they did not go out to the tent** before stating that **the Spirit rested on them, and they prophesied in the camp**. Alternate translation: [And they were among the written ones, but they did not go out to the tent. And the spirit rested on them, and they prophesied in the camp]
See how you translated the similar phrase in 11:26.

The implication is that these men were among those who had been selected and registered as leaders. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [among those whose names were written down as chosen leaders]

The expression **among the written ones** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Moses. Alternate translation: [among the ones whose names Moses had written down]

Here, the author speaks of going to the sacred tent as “going out.” However, the sacred tent was in the center of the campsite. If a speaker of your language would not use the phrase **go out** for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [but they did not approach]

27.note: The author is not referring to a **young man** who has already been mentioned in the story. He means an unidentified young man. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a certain young man]

The term **and he said** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

28.note: The word **Nun** is the name of a man.

Here, the phrase the ULT translates as **from his youth** could mean: (1) that Joshua had been ministering to Moses since Joshua was young. Alternate translation: [since he was young] (2) that Joshua was one of Moses’ “chosen,” or best, men. Alternate translation: [as one of his chosen men]

The terms **answered and said** introduce a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent both of these terms explicitly.

Joshua is referring to **Moses** by a respectful title. Use a comparable title or expression for addressing someone respectfully in your language. Alternate translation: [My master Moses] or [Moses my leader]

29.note: Moses is using the question form to rebuke Joshua’s concern. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Do not be jealous for me!]

By **Are you being jealous for me**, Moses means “Are you trying to protect my authority as leader?” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Are you trying to protect my leadership]

29.q: וּ⁠מִ֨י יִתֵּ֜ן כָּל־עַ֤ם יְהוָה֙ נְבִיאִ֔ים כִּי־יִתֵּ֧ן יְהוָ֛ה אֶת־רוּח֖⁠וֹ עֲלֵי⁠הֶֽם
29.note: Moses is using the question form to express his wish or desire that all of Yahweh’s people would be prophets. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [If only all the people of Yahweh would be prophets, that Yahweh would give his Spirit on them!]

29.q: וּ⁠מִ֨י יִתֵּ֜ן כָּל־עַ֤ם יְהוָה֙ נְבִיאִ֔ים כִּי־יִתֵּ֧ן יְהוָ֛ה אֶת־רוּח֖⁠וֹ עֲלֵי⁠הֶֽם
29.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about Yahweh giving his Spirit before the information about the people becoming prophets, since in the context, Yahweh gives his Spirit before people prophesy. Alternate translation: [And when will Yahweh give his Spirit on all the people of Yahweh, and who will give them as prophets]

Moses is using the phrase **who will give** as a common expression of his culture to mean “who will make” or “who will cause.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And who will make all the people of Yahweh prophets]
See how you translated the similar words in 11:25.

Here the word **that** introduces a second wish. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [and that]

30.q: וַ⁠יֵּאָסֵ֥ף מֹשֶׁ֖ה אֶל־הַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶ֑ה ה֖וּא וְ⁠זִקְנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
30.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **he and the elders of Israel** with the information about **Moses** at the beginning of the sentence. Alternate translation: [And Moses and the elders of Israel were gathered to the camp]

The expression **was gathered** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And Moses returned]

31.note: Here, the author is speaking as if the **wind** were actually a person that Yahweh sent on a mission. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh sent a wind]

A **quail** is a kind of small, plump game bird. If your readers would not be familiar with what a quail is, you could use the name of a similar bird that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [small, plump game birds]

The author assumes that readers will know that **the sea** refers to the Gulf of Aqaba, on the eastern side of the Sinai region. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from the nearby gulf]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and it left the quails upon the camp]

31.q: כְּ⁠דֶ֧רֶךְ י֣וֹם כֹּ֗ה וּ⁠כְ⁠דֶ֤רֶךְ יוֹם֙ כֹּ֔ה סְבִיב֖וֹת הַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶ֑ה
31.note: The phrase **as a way of a day this way and as a way of a day that way** was a common expression of this culture that means “about a day’s journey in each direction.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and about a day’s journey in each direction from the camp]

Here, the author could be indicating that: (1) the quails lay in piles on the ground, and the piles were **about two cubits** high. Alternate translation: [and in piles about two cubits high on the face of] (2) the quails were flying **about two cubits** above the ground. Alternate translation: [and flying about cubits above the face of]

The term **two cubits** refers to a unit of measurement corresponding to the distance between an average person’s elbow and middle fingertip, or about 46 centimeters or 18 inches. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express this distance in modern measurements, either in the text or a footnote. Alternate translation: [and about three feet]

Here, **face of the land** represents the surface of the ground. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [on top of the land]

32.note: The author is using **rose** as a common expression of his culture to mean “got up and started working.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the people worked]

It might seem that the expression **the day of** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and all the next day]

In this verse, the word **quail** is singular in form, but it refers to all the birds as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “quail.” Alternate translation: [the quail birds]

The implication is that even the person who gathered the least amount still gathered a very large quantity of quail. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Even the one making little gathered very much: ten homers]

The phrase **making little** is a common expression of this culture that means “doing the least work” or “gathering the least amount.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The one who did the least work]

The term **homer** was equivalent to 220 liters or about 6.5 bushels. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express this in terms of modern measurements, either in the text or in a footnote.

The author does not state why the people spread the quails around the camp. Some scholars think that they did this so that the meat from the quails would dry out and last longer. However, it is not certain that this is why they spread them out. So it is recommended that you do not explain in your translation why they spread out the quails. You could include possible interpretations in a footnote if that would be helpful to your readers.

The author is repeating forms of the verb **spread** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [And they spread widely]
The pronoun **them** refers to the Israelites who gathered the quails. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for themselves]

33.q: הַ⁠בָּשָׂ֗ר עוֹדֶ֨⁠נּוּ֙ בֵּ֣ין שִׁנֵּי⁠הֶ֔ם טֶ֖רֶם יִכָּרֵ֑ת
33.note: The expression **The flesh was still between their teeth, before it was cut off** was a common expression of this culture that means “before they had even chewed and swallowed the meat.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They were about to bite off some of the flesh and chew it]

The expression **was cut off** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the Israelites. Alternate translation: [before they cut it off]

The phrase **the nose of Yahweh burned** is a common expression of this culture that means that Yahweh is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh’s anger burned against the people] or [and Yahweh was enraged with the people]

33.q: וַ⁠יַּ֤ךְ יְהוָה֙ בָּ⁠עָ֔ם מַכָּ֖ה רַבָּ֥ה מְאֹֽד
33.note: The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh struck the people very hard]

33.q: וַ⁠יַּ֤ךְ יְהוָה֙ בָּ⁠עָ֔ם מַכָּ֖ה רַבָּ֥ה מְאֹֽד
33.note: The implication is that Yahweh caused a large number of people to die, possibly through a disease or plague. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See the discussion of the term “struck” in the Introduction to Numbers. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh caused many of the people to die] or [and Yahweh sent a terrible plague among the people]

34.q: וַ⁠יִּקְרָ֛א אֶת־שֵֽׁם־הַ⁠מָּק֥וֹם הַ⁠ה֖וּא קִבְר֣וֹת הַֽתַּאֲוָ֑ה כִּי־שָׁם֙ קָֽבְר֔וּ אֶת־הָ⁠עָ֖ם הַ⁠מִּתְאַוִּֽים
34.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [and because there they buried the people who had desired, he called the name of that place Kibroth Hattaavah]

See how you translated the similar form in 11:3. Here, the pronoun **he** could refer: (1) generically to anyone who used this name. Alternate translation: [and people called] (2) to Moses. Alternate translation: [and Moses called]

This name **Kibroth Hattaavah** sounds like the Hebrew words for “graves of desire.” This place got this name because the Israelites buried there the people who had strongly desired meat. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain this in the text of your translation or in a footnote.

35.note: The word **Hazeroth** is the name of a place in the desert. Alternate translation: [the place called Hazeroth]

The implication is that the Israelites stayed in Hazeroth, and this is where the events in chapter 12 took place. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And they camped in Hazeroth]
